extracted.intended_audience: college students and general readers studying American government and politics
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory textbook chapter describing the constitutional powers, practices, and political uses of the U.S. President (pardon, messages, veto, privileges, and relations with Congress). Intended to teach how these powers operate in law and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits of the pardon power
rubrics_metrics.description: The President may remit a fine, commute a death sentence to a term of imprisonment, or free the offender altogether; but when forfeiture of office is one of the penalties imposed, he cannot restore the offender to his former position. Though the usual process is to pardon after conviction, a pardon may be granted before or during trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure typically involves submission of application and papers to the Attorney-General and departmental review; the presidential pardon has statutory and practical limits (cannot restore forfeited office).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors and procedure considered in granting clemency
rubrics_metrics.description: In the exercise of his power of pardon, the President relies, of course, largely upon the opinions of others. The application . . . is sent to the Attorney-General, in whose department there is a pardon-clerk in charge of the preliminary stages. Usually the judge and district attorney under whose supervision the case was first tried are asked to make any statement they may choose about the merits of the case. The Attorney-General endorses on the application his opinion as to what course of action should be pursued, and the papers are then sent to the President for final determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presidents consider fairness of trial, presence of new exculpatory evidence, and severity of sentence (President Harrison: 'If the trial seems to have been fairly conducted ... and no new exculpatory evidence is produced, and the sentence does not seem to have been unduly severe, the President refuses to interfere. He cannot weigh the evidence as well as the judge and jury.'). Emotional appeals (e.g., from relatives) are common but may be denied on public-duty grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional and customary legislative function (messaging Congress)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is required by the Constitution to give to Congress from time to time information of the state of the Union and to recommend such measures as he may judge necessary and expedient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presidential message is a major public document widely read and discussed, often printed extensively in metropolitan dailies and subject to national editorial comment; it may embody party policy, stir the country, affect congressional elections, and influence whether recommendations later become law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority and rationale for executive information to Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: "From the nature and duties of the executive department,' says Story, 'he must possess more extensive sources of information ... than can belong to Congress.' . . . It is wise that those who are called upon to execute the laws should know the spirit and intention of those who have passed them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The executive is justified and expected to lay before Congress facts and information that assist deliberations and to point out evils and suggest remedies; this close association is desirable given the executive's greater access to administrative facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and authorship of the presidential message
rubrics_metrics.description: The presidential message is very often not the work of the President alone; in every case, especially of the message prepared for the opening session of Congress, the information contained in the document is largely furnished by the various departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The President treats departmental material as he sees fit—removing paragraphs, condensing, or using it as the basis for his own conclusions. Some special messages are founded on commission reports and illustrations; others are prepared primarily to promulgate the President's own views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors determining congressional treatment of presidential recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment which the President's recommendations receive varies: they may be accepted because Congress feels they are sound, because there is an effective demand in the country, because the President has party support or can bring pressure to bear by leadership or patronage, or they may be modified or rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance can depend on policy merit, public demand, presidential party influence, or political leverage; Congress's reaction is context-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal veto procedure and override rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Every bill or joint resolution must be presented to the President; if he signs it becomes a law; if he disapproves he must return it to the house in which it originated, with a statement of his objections; the house must reconsider it. A two-thirds vote of both houses is sufficient to carry the measure over the executive veto. If the President fails to return a measure within ten days (Sundays excepted) after it is presented, it becomes a law without his signature, unless Congress prevents its return by adjourning; in that case it does not become a law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The legal procedure includes presentation, return-with-objections, reconsideration, and two-thirds override; the ten-day rule and the adjournment exception are crucial to whether a bill becomes law without signature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pocket veto and related practices
rubrics_metrics.description: When Congress adjourns leaving many bills to be signed, the President may suppress quietly the bills to which he entertains objections; and this is known as the 'pocket veto.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pocket vetoes occur when Congress prevents return by adjourning; practice also distinguishes informal or irregular presentation and bills upon which messages were written; pocket vetoes have practical significance for presidential control over unfinished legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on veto power (no line-item veto) and riders practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The President does not veto single items in appropriation bills, and Congress has attached other measures — disapproved by the President — to appropriation laws, and thus forced his signature. This practice of attaching 'riders' is somewhat discredited, and is seldom employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the President lacks a constitutional power to veto individual line items, Congress can attempt to force signature by bundling measures; the practice of riders is politically controversial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political and constitutional principles guiding exercise of the veto
rubrics_metrics.description: Different views have prevailed: Jefferson contended that unless the President's mind is tolerably clear that a bill is unauthorized by the Constitution, a respect for the wisdom of the legislature would decide in favor of their opinion. General Taylor held the veto should never be exercised except in cases of clear violation of the Constitution, or manifest haste and want of consideration by Congress. Others (e.g., Jackson, Grant, Cleveland) used the veto on broader grounds, including alleged unconstitutionality, departures from principles of finance, or to invoke executive judgment and independent executive action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presidential practice varies: some presidents use veto sparingly for clear constitutional defects, others use it for policy, finance, or party-principled reasons. The veto is seen both as a constitutional safeguard and as a political instrument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential bill-handling procedure (administrative review before signature)
rubrics_metrics.description: On its passage through Congress, a bill is signed by the President of the Senate and Speaker of the House; it is then taken to the Executive Mansion and usually referred to the head of the executive department to which its subject matter relates; in case a question of constitutionality arises, the Attorney-General is consulted. The bill then goes to the President with the departmental report upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard practice involves referral to relevant department heads and legal review by the Attorney-General before the President signs or returns a bill; recommendations for amendment may accompany a vetoed bill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the veto as a political instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: The veto power, taken in connection with the message and the appointing power, is an effective political instrument in the hands of the President. By using a threat of the veto, he may secure the passage of bills which he personally favors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threats or actual vetoes influence Congressional behavior, especially on party questions; public announcements (as Roosevelt did) can be politically controversial when used before formal presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential privileges and immunity while in office
rubrics_metrics.description: No tribunal in the land has any jurisdiction over him for any offence. He cannot be arrested for any crime, no matter how serious — even murder. He may be impeached, but until judgment has been pronounced against him, he cannot be in any way restrained of his liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immunity from arrest/restraint while in office is asserted here; impeachment and subsequent judgment remain the constitutional remedies for official misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation and emoluments restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution provides that he shall receive at stated times a compensation which may not be increased or diminished during the term for which he is elected. He is forbidden, however, to receive any other emolument from the United States or from any state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Salary is fixed for the term; additional executive allowances (mansion, offices, contingent funds, travel, furnishings, etc.) are provided by appropriations but other outside emoluments are prohibited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party tie as a primary executive-legislative bond
rubrics_metrics.description: The party tie, of necessity, binds the President and the members of his party in Congress. Although they may from time to time engage in controversies, yet on fundamental matters of policy, the President and Congress must come into a sort of working agreement. The President is regarded as the leader of his party, and it is to him that the country looks for results in administration — results which can only be brought about by his cooperation with his party in Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As party leader the President issues endorsements, public appeals, and personal influence across the country to secure legislative compliance with party pledges; this is an accepted practical means of securing policy goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointing power and Senate confirmation as instruments of influence
rubrics_metrics.description: By vesting the appointing power to a large number of important offices in the hands of the President and Senate, the Constitution draws the two departments together. The extent to which the President may use his power over appointments to influence his party friends in Congress, or the extent to which the Senate may employ its confirming power to bend the President to its will, depends upon circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointments can be used as patronage to secure votes or loyalty; the Senate's confirmation role is a reciprocal lever that can influence presidential choices and behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional requests for executive information and limits of compulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: As a matter of right, Congress may call upon the executive for papers, documents, and special information of one kind or another, and in so far as the President regards these demands as reasonable and compatible with public interest he complies with them. Congress has no power, under the Constitution, to compel him to furnish papers and documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice the administration often complies because executive officers executing the laws often know more about actual conditions; however, the constitutional limit is that Congress cannot forcibly compel production of all executive papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmental chiefs' participation in drafting and advising legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Very frequently the Attorney-General ... is asked to give his opinion before a committee or to advise members of Congress on some particular matters up for legislative action. It is also sometimes the practice for heads of departments to draft complete measures, transmit them to Congress either through a friend in that body, or even directly, and secure their reference to proper committees and ultimately their passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive departments often assist drafting and explanation of bills; the President invites influential members to the White House; Congress may also attempt to advise the President by statute or resolution — all practices that create intimacy between branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriations and Treasury relation as executive-legislative linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: The Treasury Department is by law placed in a special relation to Congress; for Congress has the power to call directly upon that department for financial information without going through the form of making a request to the President. The Treasury Department collects the estimates of the amount of money required by the various executive branches and compiles these estimates in a book which is printed and submitted to Congress at the beginning of each regular session.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law of 1909 authorizing the President to review estimated expenditures and revenues and make specific recommendations to Congress shifts a large burden of responsibility to the President and increases executive influence in legislative matters concerning the budget.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposals for formal executive presence in the legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: Several times it has been suggested that the heads of departments should be given places in the legislature for the purpose of explaining and defending measures recommended by the administration and the various policies pursued in the execution of the law. A Senate committee (1881) reported in favor of giving heads of departments the right to appear in Congress, urging that such practice was no violation of the principle of separation of powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates argue admission would make information more pertinent and conclusive and help prevent disproportionate executive influence; historical practice included departmental officers appearing before the Senate to consult or explain executive business.
